transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-18
Start: 11:00 AM PDT
Duration approx: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE); Samir Patel (Redwood SE); Laura Chen (Acme CTO); Mike Ortega (Acme DevOps); Priya Raman (Acme Security)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive focused on private VPC deployment networking (PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, DNS) and runtime performance tradeoffs (latency vs throughput, KV cache, batching, quantization). Goal: confirm networking constraints and agree next steps for benchmarks and security docs.

Topics:
- PrivateLink vs VPC peering vs customer-managed NAT egress
- Subnet layout and sizing for dedicated inference nodes
- DNS and Route53 / internal name resolution for private endpoints
- Runtime performance: KV cache behavior across requests, batching strategies, quantization impacts on latency/throughput
- Tracing and metrics hooks to measure p50/p95 and token-level cost

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick off. We're here to go deep on the private VPC setup and the runtime impact. Samir is the SE who will run through the network topology and perf notes. Laura, Mike, Priya, thanks for making time.
[00:15] Laura Chen: Yep thanks Jordan. We primarily want to validate that we can run in our VPC, keep egress minimal, and meet p95 latency of, ideally, sub 300ms for short prompts. We're also worried about cost at call volumes.
[00:30] Samir Patel: Great. Quick note on nomenclature - when I say "private endpoint" I mean Redwood Private with AWS PrivateLink endpoints into your VPC, not a public internet egress. That avoids NAT for inference control plane.
[00:45] Mike Ortega: Can you explain when we'd still need NAT? I thought PrivateLink handled everything.
[00:52] Samir Patel: Good question. PrivateLink covers control plane egress to Redwood-managed control plane and model artifact pulls if you configure S3 access via VPC endpoint. But worker nodes that are customer-managed (if you choose on-prem or BYO infra) may still need outbound egress for model downloads or OS patches. Also, if you want to reach external telemetry endpoints, you'd need NAT or egress gateways.
[01:10] Priya Raman: From security: we want to avoid broad internet egress. Is it possible to lock all traffic to PrivateLink and only permit specified S3 endpoints?
[01:18] Samir Patel: Yes - we support VPC interface endpoints for control plane and S3 gateway endpoints for artifact fetches. You can restrict to a set of prefixes using S3 VPC endpoint policies. For telemetry we support sending metrics to your hosted metrics via private peering - but if you use SaaS metrics, that would be egress.
[01:35] Laura Chen: Cool. On the runtime side, Samir, you said earlier that KV cache can significantly reduce token latency for chat sessions. How sticky is the cache across requests? Do we need session affinity?
[01:45] Samir Patel: Right - our KV cache is per model-inference worker and keyed by request prefix. For chat sessions we recommend client-side session affinity to the same worker for the shortest cold-start p50. The cache is warm for repeated context and reduces per-token compute dramatically. If you have a load balancer across many worker instances and you don't have affinity, you could see cache misses which increase latency - that's the tradeoff versus throughput.
[02:10] Mike Ortega: So affinity is important. For our scale we expect thousands of concurrent short sessions - will affinity hurt throughput?
[02:18] Samir Patel: Affinity reduces effective pooling and can lower batching opportunities. We have adaptive batching: when the attached worker sees multiple concurrently queued requests it forms batches; if you route strictly to shards it may reduce batch sizes. There's a balance: use affinity for hot sessions where low latency matters; for high-throughput stateless calls, allow more spreading to increase batching efficiency and lower cost.
[02:38] Jordan Lee: To add, Redwood Optimize can recommend batching windows and affinity policies based on workload traces. We can run a short profiling job to recommend values.
[02:45] Laura Chen: We want the profiling. Also, quantization - will that affect accuracy for our med-tech prompts?
[02:52] Samir Patel: Quantization typically reduces model memory and can improve throughput, sometimes at a small quality hit depending on the model and task. For LLMs used for clinical summarization, we suggest running A/B evals: float32 baseline vs int8 qat or int8 post-train quantization. We support multiple quant levels and can pin class of quantization per rollout. We'll help run quality regression checks with your eval set.
[03:15] Priya Raman: For encryption - where are the model shards and KV cache encrypted? And is KMS used?
[03:23] Samir Patel: Model shards at rest are encrypted using customer-managed keys for Private installs (KMS/HSM). KV cache is in-memory for live workers; persistent caches if enabled can be encrypted at rest and controlled by KMS. Control plane metadata can be configured to use your KMS for key wrapping in Private. We'll include specifics in the security checklist.
[03:45] Mike Ortega: Back to VPC routing - what do you recommend for subnets? Private subnets for workers, public for NAT?
[03:52] Samir Patel: Typical pattern: put Redwood worker ENIs or PrivateLink endpoints in private subnets across multiple AZs. Have a small public subnet with NAT gateway or egress NAT instances if you want controlled outbound. If you want zero internet egress, use VPC endpoints for S3 and PrivateLink for control/API. You may still need a managed path for OS updates - we can schedule that during maintenance windows or use S3 pre-signed artifact pulls initiated from within Redwood if you prefer zero egress.
[04:20] Laura Chen: What about DNS? We use Route53 private hosted zones. Will that work with the interface endpoints?
[04:28] Samir Patel: Yes, Route53 private hosted zones work. For AWS PrivateLink we recommend creating AWS-managed private DNS names so the endpoint resolves to the interface endpoint IPs in your VPC. Alternatively, you can use custom internal DNS entries pointing to the interface endpoint IPs. Just make sure split-horizon rules don't conflict with public resolution.
[04:48] Mike Ortega: Any issues with cross-account PrivateLink? We have infra in a different account than some of our teams.
[04:55] Samir Patel: We support cross-account endpoint setup - you create the interface endpoint in the consuming account and accept the endpoint service from the Redwood side. We'll provide the service name and the account to accept. There are primitives for allowlist and security group locking down source IPs.
[05:10] Laura Chen: Regarding latency - you said p95 target 300ms earlier. What numbers are realistic for a 1-2k token prompt on a 40B model with int8 quant and batching?
[05:22] Samir Patel: Ballpark: for short prompts (<= 64 tokens) on an optimized runtime, p50 can be 80-120ms and p95 ~180-350ms depending on batching and network hops. For 1-2k tokens, generation time dominates - per-token latency and throughput matter. Quantization can shrink per-token compute; batching increases throughput but adds queuing latency. We'll capture exact numbers by running a sample job in your VPC.
[05:46] Mike Ortega: Do you have examples of network overhead introduced by PrivateLink in ms?
[05:50] Samir Patel: PrivateLink adds minimal overhead - usually single-digit ms within region, depending on AZ routing. The bigger source of variance is crossing AZs or if you're routing through NAT or a transit gateway. Keep endpoints and workers in same AZ for lowest tail latency.
[06:05] Priya Raman: Any recommendations for security groups and least privilege?
[06:10] Samir Patel: Yes - lock down interface endpoint SG to only allow inbound from your worker subnets on the ports we document (HTTPS/443). Egress rules from worker subnets should be as restrictive as possible. Use endpoint policies to restrict S3 access; enable flow logs for auditing. We'll share a baseline terraform snippet.
[06:28] Jordan Lee: We'll attach our sample terraform and a minimal cloudformation example in the follow-up.
[06:33] Laura Chen: About fault tolerance - if a worker AZ loses capacity, can Redwood route to backup AZs? How does that interact with affinity and cache?
[06:41] Samir Patel: We support multi-AZ worker pools with automatic failover. On failover you'll get cache misses as sessions shift AZs - that's expected, and we'll see a spike in p95 for affected sessions until caches warm. To minimize impact we recommend sticky sessions with local sticky caches for short-lived sessions plus global KV cache for checkpointing where feasible, but global KV increases complexity and cross-AZ latency.
[07:06] Mike Ortega: Hmm that tradeoff is important. Is global KV something you manage or we manage?
[07:12] Samir Patel: For Private we can offer an optional managed external KV (Redis-ish) in your VPC that all workers talk to - that gives better cache hit across AZs but adds network latency for each cache op. Typically customers prefer local in-memory cache for latency-sensitive workloads and accept misses on failover.
[07:30] Laura Chen: For our clinical workflows low tail latency is more important than absolute throughput. So we'd prefer affinity and local cache.
[07:36] Samir Patel: Good call. We'll tune the autoscaling and worker-to-session ratio to ensure capacity. Also, set a warmup policy to pre-warm workers for expected traffic spikes.
[07:47] Jordan Lee: On billing and dedicated capacity - if you pick Dedicated Reserved you get pinned capacity and SLA for latency. That helps with predictability but costs more.
[07:56] Laura Chen: We'll evaluate. For the trial we want to run benchmarks with production-like prompts. Samir, can you outline the benchmark plan?
[08:03] Samir Patel: Plan: 1) ingest sample prompts (you provide ~2k prompts representative), 2) run three profiles: low-latency affinity (small batch windows), high-throughput batched, and mixed traffic. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 tokens, tokens/sec, and per-request cost estimate. We'll run via PrivateLink into your VPC and record network traces.
[08:26] Mike Ortega: We'll provide prompts. Also note we have an internal egress filtering appliance, so we need to test with that in the path.
[08:33] Samir Patel: Noted - we'll include that in the network test.
[08:37] Priya Raman: On compliance - can Redwood sign a data processing addendum for HIPAA?
[08:42] Jordan Lee: Yes, we have a HIPAA-ready offering for Private deployments; support for BAA and SOC2. We'll route legal to share the DPA/BAA in parallel.
[08:52] Laura Chen: One concern: DNS leaks - if a worker resolves external hosts, could that leak to public DNS?
[08:58] Samir Patel: If you use private hosted zones and controlled egress, DNS should be constrained. The main leak vector is when endpoint resolution falls back to public; ensure the private hosted zone has precedence. We'll send a checklist of DNS settings to verify.
[09:12] Mike Ortega: For the egress pattern, we might prefer a NAT-only egress through a proxy that logs egress - how does Redwood support proxying egress?
[09:21] Samir Patel: Workers can be configured to route outbound through your proxy. For Private installs we can provide configuration templates to use an HTTP proxy or egress appliance; we'll need to validate TLS intercept concerns.
[09:33] Jordan Lee: Quick administrative note - Samir will need the VPC IDs and account numbers to generate the PrivateLink service name. Mike, can you share those?
[09:41] Mike Ortega: I'll collect and share post-call; it'll take until EOD tomorrow.
[09:45] Samir Patel: Great. For the benchmarking environment, we'll need IAM permissions scoped for S3 read-only for model artifacts, and ability to create interface endpoints in consuming account. We'll document exact minimal permissions.
[09:59] Laura Chen: For devops, how is autoscaling handled for Dedicated in Private? Is it automatic?
[10:05] Samir Patel: Autoscaling is configurable; for Dedicated we can set target CPU/GPU queue thresholds and scale policy. Scaling actions take minutes because we're provisioning GPU nodes; rapid bursts use burst capacity if configured. For strict p95 targets we recommend some headroom in the reserve.
[10:22] Priya Raman: Monitoring - do you export traces to our X-Ray/Datadog?
[10:27] Samir Patel: We have integrations - can push traces to Datadog or to your Jaeger/X-Ray collector in your VPC; requires you to provide the collector endpoint and we can use private connectivity.
[10:38] Jordan Lee: We're getting toward the end. Let's recap next steps.
[10:42] Laura Chen: Recap: Acme to share VPC IDs, subnets, and sample prompts; Redwood to send checklist and run benchmark; schedule follow-up SRE deep-dive.
[10:50] Jordan Lee: Correct. Mike you'll share details; Samir will run bench; I'll share SOC2 and BAA paperwork with legal.
[10:59] Mike Ortega: I'll get the account IDs and subnets today or tomorrow.
[11:03] Priya Raman: Please include DNS checklist in the security docs.
[11:07] Jordan Lee: Will do. Thanks everyone.
[11:10] Laura Chen: Thanks.
[11:12] End of recording.
